explanation: Fires most clearly on the second half of a fixed pair of opposites, such as 'after' in 'before and after', 'down' in 'up and down', 'South' in 'North and South' and '-west' in 'east-west'. It also fires about as strongly on unrelated middle subword pieces of long or technical words ('Lore[nt]z', 'b[ary]onic', 'Tri[ang]ulation', 'Elek[tron]ik') and on the month digit in ISO dates ('2013-[0]5'). Ordinary tokens get little or no activation.

Fires on the particle or object that completes an idiomatic verb phrase, where the verb comes just before it: 'throw out [there]', 'bring it [on]', 'sell anyone [on]', 'turn on each [other]', 'run am[ok]', 'take with [you]', 'fly [up]', 'dressed up [as]'. It also fires on verb particles in other languages (Hungarian 'hívta [fel]', German 'dah[inter]'). The same words outside such a phrase fire weakly.

Fires on a subword piece in the middle of a word, especially in proper names (Shim-ura, Tec-um-seh, Anton-in, Katan) and in words from languages other than English (German 'wieder-h-olt', Portuguese 'n-enh-uma', Swedish 'h-itt-ades', Hungarian). Whole common English words fire weakly or not at all.

Fires on negation words and prefixes: 'not', 'no', 'n't', 'without', 'un-', 'anti-', 'never' and negative verbs like 'avoid' or 'remove' after 'must not'. It is strongest on 'not' in license boilerplate ('you may [not] use this file'). Weaker on 'of' in 'lack of' or 'out of'. Non-negative tokens get nothing.

The top examples share no clear pattern. They include Portuguese and French function words ('no', 'en', 'alguns'), the first piece of place or person names ('Som'erville, 'Carlo'), 'take'/'took' in 'take place', commas and periods in lists or version numbers, and 'like' or 'in' after a noun phrase. I could not find a rule that predicts it.

Fires on tokens inside formal notation: LaTeX math (variable names, subscripts, '$', braces and parentheses inside $...$) and code (type names, parameters, CSS property names, assignment lines). A few science words naming a quantity ('radius', 'activity') fire moderately. Plain prose fires weakly or not at all.

Fires on the comma that closes a sentence-initial adverb or introductory phrase before the main clause ('However,', 'Therefore,', 'In this case,', 'In 1998,', 'Now,'). Other commas, such as after a clause or in an appositive, fire moderately, and so does the complementizer 'that' after verbs like 'ruled' or 'remains'. Most other tokens give nothing.

Fires on the infinitive 'to' that introduces a purpose or goal clause ('in order to', 'taxes to fund', 'how to', 'battle to sell', 'tools to strengthen', and sentence-initial 'To ...'). It also fires on nearby verbs in the same construction ('helped' to lower, 'to be kept') and, somewhat, on '-f' word fragments ('-fighting', 'foment'). A 'to' that is a preposition fires much less.

Fires on tokens in running text in languages other than English, mostly European languages written in the Latin alphabet (Italian, Romanian, Portuguese, Danish, Finnish, Estonian, Vietnamese). It is strongest on function words or word-initial pieces near the start of a clause ('per', 'Nu', 'P-elo', 'não', 'không'). It is moderate on foreign proper names inside English text and weak on other scripts and English.

Mixed. Its most common trigger is the decimal point or thousands separator inside a number or version string ('345[.]6', 'Kv1[.]1', 'RSS 2[.]0', '2[,]000', 'W[.] 132'). It also fires on the subject pronoun or word that starts a main clause after a long subordinate phrase with no comma ('at the same time [we] make', 'at the sandwich [he] found'), and on other scattered tokens. Plain prose tokens are weak.

Fires on an abstract head noun right after 'the' in a 'the X of' construction, most strongly on 'nature' ('the nature of', 'the serious nature of', 'forces of nature'). 'death' ('the death of') and similar nouns such as 'interest' and 'usual' fire somewhat less. Existential 'there' fires moderately. Other nouns give little.
